D1 — Add gstack skill routing rules to this project's CLAUDE.md?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: gstack works best when your project's CLAUDE.md includes skill routing rules. Routing rules are a short list telling Claude which /skill to run for which kind of request (bugs → /investigate, ship → /ship, and so on), so you don't have to remember skill names. This is a one-time setup prompt per project and has nothing to do with the auth plan itself.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without rules you invoke skills by hand; with them, CLAUDE.md grows by ~15 lines. Either way the plan review is unaffected.
Recommendation: A because it makes the rest of gstack discoverable at near-zero cost, and this is a setup step, not an engineering remedy.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Add routing rules to CLAUDE.md (recommended)
  ✅ Future requests auto-route to the right skill without remembering names
  ✅ Teammates who clone the repo get the same routing behavior from day one
  ❌ Adds a ~15-line section to CLAUDE.md; in plan mode the edit and commit wait until plan mode exits
B) No thanks, I'll invoke skills manually
  ✅ CLAUDE.md stays exactly as it is; nothing to commit
  ✅ You keep full manual control over when skills run
  ❌ You have to remember and type skill names yourself; this prompt is suppressed for the project afterward
Net: a discoverability convenience versus a slightly longer CLAUDE.md; the review itself is unchanged either way.

D2 — Let gstack search learnings from your other projects on this machine?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: gstack saves small lessons from each review session (a pitfall, a pattern that worked). It can either look only at this project's lessons, or also at lessons saved from your other projects on this same machine. Nothing leaves your machine either way. Cross-project is useful for a solo dev whose projects rhyme; it is a bad idea when you work on multiple client codebases and don't want one client's patterns influencing another's review.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too narrow means a lesson learned elsewhere (say, about shared mutable caches) never resurfaces here. Too wide means unrelated client context leaks into recommendations.
Recommendation: A because for a single developer the extra recall is free and local, and there is nothing to contaminate today (0 learnings on file).
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Enable cross-project learnings (recommended)
  ✅ Past pitfalls from any of your projects surface when a finding matches them
  ✅ Stays fully local; it is a config flag you can flip back with one command
  ❌ Patterns from unrelated codebases could color recommendations here
B) Keep learnings project-scoped only
  ✅ Strict isolation between codebases, right for multi-client work
  ✅ Recommendations only ever cite lessons from this repo
  ❌ Slower compounding; every project relearns the same pitfalls
Net: recall breadth versus codebase isolation; a one-line config either way.

questions.question:
D4 — Where does the Promise.all IDP speedup belong relative to the refactor?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: The plan says its goal is to reorganize auth code without changing what it does (PLAN.md:7-8), and then also proposes making 5 identity-provider calls run at once instead of one after another (PLAN.md:39-40). Those are two different kinds of change. A pure reorganization can be checked with "same inputs, same outputs". A speedup changes timing, which error the user sees first when two calls fail, and how hard the IDP gets hit. Mixing them in one commit means when something breaks you can't tell which change did it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Bundled: a login regression could be either the reorg or the parallelization and you bisect blind. Deferred forever: users keep waiting ~5x the necessary time on every token validation.
Recommendation: A because the speedup is real and cheap, but it must land as its own commit after the reorg is green against regression tests (Beck: separate structural from behavioral change).
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Keep in scope, sequenced as its own commit after the reorg + regression tests are green (recommended) (human: ~2h / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Users get the latency win in this same branch, not a someday follow-up
  ✅ Each commit is independently bisectable; a failure points at one change
  ❌ One more sequencing constraint the implementer has to respect
B) Defer to a follow-up PR / TODO
  ✅ This branch stays a pure reorg with a clean same-in-same-out proof
  ✅ Zero risk that IDP rate limits or error-ordering changes ship with the reorg
  ❌ Latency win waits on a second review cycle; follow-ups often never happen
C) Bundle into the refactor as the plan currently proposes
  ✅ Fewest commits; implementer touches token validation once
  ✅ No sequencing rule to enforce
  ❌ Structural and behavioral change in one diff; a regression is ambiguous to attribute, and "no behavior change" stops being true
Net: same code either way; the choice is whether the speedup is bisectable from the reorg.

options.label: Keep in scope, own commit after reorg is green (recommended)
options.description: Parallelization stays in this branch but lands as a separate commit sequenced after the reorg and its regression coverage pass.

options.label: Defer to follow-up PR / TODO
options.description: Remove parallelization from this plan; capture it as a TODO with context. Branch stays a pure structural refactor.

options.label: Bundle into the refactor as proposed
options.description: Implement Promise.all inside the same commits as the reorg, as PLAN.md currently describes.

questions.question:
D5 — Five new classes, or a smaller arrangement with the same behavior?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: The plan adds five new classes across 12 files (PLAN.md:43-44) to reorganize code that is not supposed to change behavior. Two of them look like ceremony. RequestPolicy is described as a stateless allow/deny decision with no network, cache, or state (PLAN.md:8-12); that is a function, not a class. TokenStore is named once and never described: no responsibility, no caller, and its name overlaps with AuthCache, which already stores validated tokens through the existing adapter (PLAN.md:15-21). Every extra class is another seam to mock, another file to read at 3am, and another place for the token lifecycle to drift.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too many classes: two components with overlapping token storage responsibilities and a mock surface with nothing behind it. Too few: if TokenStore actually has a distinct job (say, refresh-token persistence), collapsing it hides a real boundary.
Recommendation: A because RequestPolicy has no state by the author's own description, and TokenStore has no stated job; both fold away with zero feature loss. Restore TokenStore only if a written responsibility appears that AuthCache cannot own.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Three classes + one pure function: AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache; requestPolicy.decide(claims, ctx) as a module function; TokenStore folded into AuthCache (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ One owner for token storage, one seam (AuthCache) to inject in tests
  ✅ Policy decision is a pure function: table-driven tests, no mocks, trivially DRY
  ❌ If TokenStore later needs a separate lifecycle (e.g. refresh tokens), it gets extracted then instead of now
B) Keep all five classes as planned
  ✅ Matches the author's original decomposition; no re-planning
  ✅ Each concept gets its own file and test module
  ❌ TokenStore ships with no written contract, overlapping AuthCache; RequestPolicy is a class wrapper around a stateless function
C) Four classes: fold RequestPolicy to a pure function, keep TokenStore pending a written responsibility
  ✅ Removes the clearest ceremony (stateless class) immediately
  ✅ Preserves TokenStore in case the author has an unstated distinct job for it
  ❌ Ships an undefined class boundary; "we'll define it later" is how overlap becomes permanent
Net: fewer seams and one token owner versus preserving an undescribed boundary that might turn out to matter.

options.label: 3 classes + pure requestPolicy fn (recommended)
options.description: AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache as classes. RequestPolicy becomes a module-level pure function. TokenStore folded into AuthCache. Same behavior, same retained contracts.

options.label: Keep all five classes as planned
options.description: AuthBroker, TokenStore, SessionMint, AuthCache, RequestPolicy as five classes across 12 files, per PLAN.md:43-44.

questions.question:
D6 — How do AuthBroker and SessionMint get their AuthCache: injected, or imported as a module-level global?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: The plan has both new services import one shared AuthCache object from a module (PLAN.md:27-28). That works, but it is a hidden dependency: anyone reading AuthBroker cannot see it depends on the cache, every test in the process shares the same cache state, and you cannot run two brokers with different caches. Constructor injection means the app builds one AuthCache at startup and hands it to both services. Same single backing cache in production (the retained contract at PLAN.md:20), but tests get a fresh one per test and the dependency is visible in the signature.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Module global: test pollution between test files (a token cached in one test leaks into the next), and a future second tenant pool cannot get its own cache without a rewrite. Injection: a few extra constructor lines and one composition-root file.
Recommendation: A because explicit-over-clever is the stated preference, the search check flagged module singletons as the standard footgun, and the retained one-backing-cache contract is preserved by constructing exactly one instance at the root.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Constructor injection from a composition root (recommended) (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Dependency is visible in the constructor; tests pass a fresh AuthCache with no global reset hooks
  ✅ Single production instance is still guaranteed by building it once at the root
  ❌ One more file (the composition root) and constructor plumbing in both services
B) Keep the module-level exported instance as proposed
  ✅ Zero plumbing; import and go, matches the original plan text
  ✅ Trivially guarantees a single instance without a root
  ❌ Hidden coupling; shared mutable state across every test and request in the process; no way to isolate
C) Module default export plus optional constructor override
  ✅ Production code stays import-and-go while tests can inject
  ✅ Smaller diff than a full composition root
  ❌ Two ways to obtain the cache; the default path still hides the dependency and invites drift between test and prod wiring
Net: a visible, injectable dependency versus the convenience of a global; the single-cache contract holds either way.

options.label: Constructor injection from a composition root (recommended)
options.description: Build one AuthCache at app startup and pass it into AuthBroker and SessionMint constructors. Tests construct their own.

options.label: Keep module-level exported instance
options.description: Both services import the shared AuthCache from its module, as PLAN.md:27-28 proposes.

options.label: Module default + optional override
options.description: Export a default instance; constructors accept an optional AuthCache that defaults to it.

questions.question:
D7 — With two services writing to one cache, who is allowed to mutate it, and is a late write after invalidation rejected?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: Today the plan lets both AuthBroker and SessionMint write into the cache directly, and the plan itself says the cache does not serialize writes (PLAN.md:18, 28). Picture this: an admin suspends a tenant, the cache is wiped for that tenant, but SessionMint was mid-flight (waiting on the identity provider) and finishes a moment later, writing a fresh valid session for the suspended tenant. That tenant stays logged in until the entry expires. The fix has two parts you can pick separately: route all writes through AuthCache's own named methods (one owner, one place to reason about), and have AuthCache stamp each write with the tenant's invalidation generation so a write that started before a suspension is dropped.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without a guard, a suspended or revoked tenant can regain access for up to one TTL in a race that is rare in tests and common at scale. Over-engineering risk is small: the guard is one counter per tenant inside the facade.
Recommendation: A because this is auth, the race is a security fail-open, and the guard is ~20 lines in the facade plus one race test; the adapter stays untouched.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) Single writer (AuthCache intent methods) + per-tenant generation guard (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Closes the resurrection-after-invalidation window; suspension and revocation are immediately final
  ✅ One owner for key construction, so tenant/issuer/audience/policy-version keys are built in exactly one place (DRY)
  ❌ Requires AuthCache to observe invalidation (subscribe to adapter hooks or route invalidation through the facade); if hooks are not observable this needs a small hook
B) Single writer (AuthCache intent methods), no generation guard
  ✅ One owner and DRY key construction with the smallest facade surface
  ✅ No dependency on observing adapter invalidation events
  ❌ The resurrection race stays open; a suspended tenant can be re-cached by an in-flight mint
C) Services mutate directly through pass-through methods, as proposed
  ✅ Least code; the facade is a thin alias over the adapter
  ✅ Nothing new to learn for anyone who knows the adapter
  ❌ Two writers building keys independently, no place to enforce write rules, and the race is open
Net: closing a real auth fail-open for ~20 lines in the facade versus keeping the facade thin and accepting the race.

options.label: Single writer + per-tenant generation guard (recommended)
options.description: Only AuthCache mutates the adapter, through intent-named methods. Each write carries the tenant invalidation generation captured at operation start; stale writes are rejected. Adapter unchanged.

options.label: Single writer, no generation guard
options.description: Only AuthCache mutates, through intent-named methods. No stale-write rejection; the race window is documented.

options.label: Direct pass-through mutation as proposed
options.description: AuthBroker and SessionMint call get/set/delete on the cache directly.

questions.question:
D8 — Flatten validateAndDispatch() into a step pipeline with one error boundary, or patch the three nested catches in place?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: The new validateAndDispatch() is described as 60 lines with three try/catch blocks nested inside each other, each one quietly eating a different kind of error (PLAN.md:31-32). "Swallowing" means the function keeps going after a step failed. In an auth path that is the dangerous direction: if the identity-provider call fails and gets swallowed, the request can continue toward dispatch with incomplete validation. The fix is to make every failure produce an explicit, named outcome (deny, auth-unavailable, or rethrow) and to lay the function out as a straight line of small named steps so a tired engineer can read it top to bottom at 3am. Which outcome each error maps to is not our call here: it must match what legacyAuthFlow() does today, which the regression fixtures (R4) will pin down.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Swallowed errors in auth are a fail-open waiting to happen and are invisible in logs. Flattening costs a few extraction moves; patching in place leaves the 60-line nest that produced the swallows in the first place.
Recommendation: A because the nesting is the root cause of the swallows, extraction is cheap with CC, and one error boundary is the only place where "which error maps to which outcome" can be verified against the regression fixtures.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) Linear step pipeline with one top-level error boundary; every error class maps to an explicit outcome matching legacy (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Each step is a ~10-line named function with its own unit tests; the error mapping is a single table you can diff against legacy
  ✅ No silent continuation: an IDP failure cannot reach dispatch
  ❌ More small functions to name; the diff is larger than an in-place patch
B) Keep the nested structure; replace each swallow with an explicit outcome
  ✅ Smallest diff that removes the fail-open behavior
  ✅ No renaming or extraction to review
  ❌ Three nested boundaries remain, so the error mapping is spread across the function and the next swallow is one edit away
C) Keep as proposed (nested catches that swallow)
  ✅ Zero extra work now
  ✅ Matches the author's draft exactly
  ❌ Silent failures in the auth path; nothing tells you a validation step failed
Net: a readable pipeline with one verifiable error table versus a minimal patch on a structure that invites the same bug back.

options.label: Linear pipeline, one error boundary, explicit outcomes (recommended)
options.description: Extract validate / cache lookup / policy / dispatch into named steps; one top-level boundary maps each error class to an explicit outcome that matches legacyAuthFlow()'s captured behavior.

options.label: Keep nesting, make each catch explicit
options.description: Leave the three nested try/catch blocks; change each catch to return an explicit outcome instead of swallowing.

options.label: Keep as proposed
options.description: Ship the 60-line function with three swallowing catches.

answers.D8 — Flatten validateAndDispatch() into: Linear pipeline, one error boundary, explicit outcomes (recommended)

questions.question:
D9 — How do we prove the rewrite behaves like legacyAuthFlow(): full characterization suite, a reduced one, or characterization plus a production shadow-compare?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: The plan rewrites the function that decides whether every request is allowed in, and says it will not test that the new version behaves like the old one (PLAN.md:35-36). A characterization test is simple: before touching anything, feed the old function a table of inputs (good token, expired token, wrong tenant, revoked, suspended tenant, identity provider down, and so on) and record exactly what comes out, including what ends up in the cache. Then run the same table against the new code. If both agree on every row, the "no behavior change" promise is proven rather than hoped. The question is how wide the table is, and whether you also want a live safety net in production.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too narrow: a tenant-isolation or revocation regression ships and you learn about it from a customer. Too wide: a day of test writing for a human team, though minutes with CC.
Recommendation: A because this is auth for multiple tenants, every row in the matrix is a real production input, and the whole suite is ~20 table rows that CC writes in minutes; shadow-compare (C) is a good add only if you have traffic diversity the matrix cannot enumerate.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=10/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full characterization suite across the whole input matrix, captured before the rewrite (recommended) (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Proves "no behavior change" row by row, including cache state and IDP call counts, and doubles as the permanent regression suite
  ✅ Any pre-existing fail-open in legacy is discovered before the rewrite, not after
  ❌ Requires a small test double for the IDP and adapter to make every row deterministic
B) Reduced matrix: happy path, expired token, policy deny, one IDP failure
  ✅ Fast to write and covers the four most common outcomes
  ✅ Still proves the main flow survived the rewrite
  ❌ Cross-tenant, revocation, suspension and concurrency rows are exactly where multi-tenant auth breaks, and they are untested
C) Full characterization suite plus a flagged production shadow-compare for one release (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1.5 h)
  ✅ Catches input shapes no one thought to put in the table, with real traffic
  ✅ Fully reversible: the flag removes the shadow path with no code change
  ❌ Doubles IDP load while the shadow runs and adds a temporary code path that must be removed later
Net: a complete, cheap, permanent proof versus a quicker partial one; shadow-compare buys real-traffic coverage at the cost of temporary ops complexity.

options.label: Full characterization suite (recommended)
options.description: Capture legacyAuthFlow()'s observable behavior across the full input matrix before the rewrite; run the same suite against the new code; delete legacy only when both pass.

options.label: Reduced characterization matrix
options.description: Same mechanism, four rows: valid, expired, policy deny, IDP timeout.

options.label: Full suite + production shadow-compare
options.description: Option A plus a flagged shadow path that runs both implementations and logs diffs for one release.

questions.question:
D10 — Capture "single-flight dedupe for concurrent same-token validations" as a TODO?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-aL5jl6 on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: When the same token arrives twice at once (double-click, two tabs), both requests miss the cache and each fires its own 5 identity-provider calls. Single-flight means AuthCache keeps one in-flight promise per cache key so the second caller waits on the first result instead of repeating the work. It is a real IDP-load and latency win, but it changes concurrency behavior, so it does not belong in a "no behavior change" refactor.
What: add in-flight request coalescing (one pending validation per cache key) inside AuthCache.
Why: halves or better the IDP call volume under bursty duplicate traffic; removes duplicate-session races.
Pros: fewer IDP calls, lower p99 under storms, natural home now that AuthCache is the single writer (D7).
Cons: a new concurrency primitive in the auth path; needs its own race tests; interacts with the generation guard (a coalesced result must still be rejected if the tenant was invalidated mid-flight).
Context: after this refactor, AuthCache is the only component that touches the adapter, so the in-flight map has exactly one owner. Start in AuthCache.lookupOrValidate; reuse the R4 concurrency row as the test seed.
Depends on / blocked by: this refactor landing first (D5 structure, D7 single writer).
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skip and the idea is lost until a load incident; build now and the refactor stops being behavior-neutral.
Recommendation: A because it is valuable, clearly out of scope for a behavior-neutral refactor, and the reasoning above is worth preserving.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
  ✅ Preserves the motivation and starting point for whoever picks it up in three months
  ✅ Keeps this branch a pure reorg plus one isolated perf commit
  ❌ TODOS.md must be created after plan mode exits; nothing ships now
B) Skip, not valuable enough
  ✅ Nothing to maintain or track
  ✅ Avoids speculative work if duplicate-token bursts are rare in your traffic
  ❌ The load analysis above is lost and gets rediscovered during an incident
C) Build it now in this PR
  ✅ Users get the latency and IDP-load win immediately
  ✅ AuthCache is already being written, so the code is adjacent
  ❌ Adds a second behavioral change to a refactor whose proof is "same in, same out"; expands scope the complexity gate just reduced
Net: capturing a well-reasoned follow-up versus dropping it or widening scope right after narrowing it.

## Step 0: Scope Challenge

**Evidence note:** this repo contains only `PLAN.md` and `CLAUDE.md`; there is no implementation code to probe, so every finding below quotes the plan (file:line) and runtime evidence is recorded as unknown. Nothing here is an observed regression; these are proposal risks.

**1. What already exists / can be reused**

D8 — Flatten validateAndDispatch() into a step pipeline with one error boundary, or patch the three nested catches in place?

A characterization test is simple: before touching anything, feed the old function a table of inputs (good token, expired token, wrong tenant, revoked, suspended tenant, identity provider down, and so on) and record exactly what comes out, including what ends up in the cache. The question is how wide the table is, and whether you also want a live safety net in production.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too narrow: a tenant-isolation or revocation regression ships and you learn about it from a customer. Too wide: a day of test writing for a human team, though minutes with CC.
Recommendation: A because this is auth for multiple tenants, every row in the matrix is a real production input, and the whole suite is ~20 table rows that CC writes in minutes; shadow-compare (C) is a good add only if you have traffic diversity the matrix cannot enumerate.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=10/10

A) Full characterization suite across the whole input matrix, captured before the rewrite (recommended) (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Proves "no behavior change" row by row, including cache state and IDP call counts, and doubles as the permanent regression suite
  ✅ Any pre-existing fail-open in legacy is discovered before the rewrite, not after
  ❌ Requires a small test double for the IDP and adapter to make every row deterministic
B) Reduced matrix: happy path, expired token, policy deny, one IDP failure
  ✅ Fast to write and covers the four most common outcomes
  ✅ Still proves the main flow survived the rewrite
  ❌ Cross-tenant, revocation, suspension and concurrency rows are exactly where multi-tenant auth breaks, and they are untested

  ✅ Fully reversible: the flag removes the shadow path with no code change
  ❌ Doubles IDP load while the shadow runs and adds a temporary code path that must be removed later
Net: a complete, cheap, permanent proof versus a quicker partial one; shadow-compare buys real-traffic coverage at the cost of temporary ops complexity.
